title: Don't Forget to Elaborate
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: While explicit instruction and retrieval practice form the foundation of learning, students also require elaboration—the active process of adding meaningful connections, analysis, and reflection to newly absorbed information. Research shows that elaboration tasks deepen both comprehension and long-term retention beyond what retrieval practice alone can achieve. The core pedagogical challenge is balancing the groundwork of direct instruction with higher-order thinking activities, carefully tailored to match each student's knowledge level and readiness. Elaboration operates across multiple modalities: guided writing with sentence stems, strategic questioning that prompts analysis, and structured discussion. Critically, elaboration is not an advanced enrichment strategy reserved for high-achieving students—it is essential for all learners, including those carrying gaps in background knowledge. When designed properly, elaboration closes understanding gaps rather than widening them.
points: Elaboration involves making new connections between texts, texts and prior knowledge, or answering how/why/example questions
Studies show elaboration improves both retention and comprehension, whereas retrieval practice alone addresses retention only
Elaboration can be taught through scaffolded writing with sentence stems, reducing cognitive load
Elaboration works effectively with students who have learning challenges if tasks are carefully designed
Teachers should embed coherent writing instruction across content areas to ensure students engage in both retrieval practice and elaboration
quotes: Elaboration simply means adding something to information you've absorbed. That could consist of making a connection between different texts or between a text and a student's pre-existing knowledge or opinions.
We want students to engage in deep, meaningful, thoughtful processing. And that is what we really mean when we're talking about elaboration.
Only the two groups who engaged in elaboration—by coming up with their own examples—achieved deeper comprehension.
Elaborative activities are what all students need to realize their full academic and cognitive potential.

One relatively simple way to ensure that students are engaging in both retrieval practice and elaboration is to have teachers embed a coherent method of writing instruction in whatever content they're teaching.” Archived from Minding the Gap on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
